title: Graph basics & the three ways to store a graph
overview: The algorithms course opens with graphs: dots (nodes) joined by lines (edges). Before you can search a graph you must store it in memory. This module builds the three standard storages, adjacency matrix, adjacency list and edge list, and shows when each one is handy.

concepts.explain: A node is a thing (a city, a person). An edge is a link between two nodes. We usually number nodes `0` to `n-1` so they can be array indexes.
In an undirected graph an edge `a b` can be walked both ways, so we store it twice (`a→b` and `b→a`). In a directed graph we store only `a→b`.
An `n x n` table where `mat[a][b] = 1` means there is an edge from `a` to `b`. Checking one edge is O(1), but it always uses n² memory.
An array of vectors: `adj[a]` holds every neighbour of `a`. Memory is O(n + e) and it is the storage used by BFS/DFS in later modules.
Just a list of `(a, b)` pairs. Very simple, and it is exactly what Bellman-Ford and Kruskal want later.
When an edge has a cost, store it next to the neighbour, e.g. `pair<int,int>{b, cost}` (you will see this in Module 6).

files.title: Adjacency matrix (directed)
files.what: Reads a directed graph and stores it in a 2D array `adj_mat`, then prints the whole table.
steps: Read `n` (nodes) and `e` (edges) and make an `n x n` array `adj_mat`.
Fill every cell with `0` using two loops (the commented `memset` line is the shortcut).
A loop sets `adj_mat[i][i] = 1` for every node `i < n`: an optional mark meaning a node can reach itself.
For each edge `a b`, set only `adj_mat[a][b] = 1`, because the edge points one way.
Print the table row by row: row = from, column = to.
files.input_note: First line `n e`, then `e` lines `a b` meaning an arrow a → b.
files.output_note: Row 2 is `1 0 1 1`: from node 2 you can go to 0 and 3 (and the diagonal 1 is the self mark). Row 0 has a 1 in column 1 but row 1 has a 0 in column 0, because arrows are one-way.
files.watch_out: The diagonal 1s are only a convention ("a node reaches itself"). Many problems want the diagonal left at 0, so drop that loop when a problem does not ask for self marks.

check.q: How do you know from the matrix that an edge is directed?
check.a: `mat[a][b]` is 1 but `mat[b][a]` is 0: the table is not symmetric.

files.title: Adjacency matrix (undirected)
files.what: Same as the directed version, but every edge is written in both directions so the table is symmetric.
steps: Read `n` and `e`, create `adj_mat` and fill it with zeros.
Mark the diagonal with one `adj_mat[i][i] = 1` per node (same optional convention as the directed file).
For each edge `a b` set both `adj_mat[a][b]` and `adj_mat[b][a]` to 1.
Print the table.
files.input_note: First line `n e`, then `e` lines `a b`.
files.output_note: A symmetric table: row 0 is `1 1 1 0` and column 0 reads the same top to bottom. Row 3 is `0 0 1 1`: node 3 touches only node 2 (plus its own diagonal mark).
files.watch_out: A variable-length array like `int adj_mat[n][n]` must be declared with both sizes; forgetting a bracket (`adj_mat][n]`) is a compile error. Also make the diagonal loop run to `n` (nodes), not `e` (edges).

check.q: Why is an undirected adjacency matrix always symmetric?
check.a: Each edge `a b` sets both `mat[a][b]` and `mat[b][a]`.

files.title: Adjacency list (undirected)
files.what: Stores the graph as an array of vectors, one vector of neighbours per node, and prints each node's list.
steps: `vector<int> adj_list[n];` gives one empty vector per node.
For each edge `a b`, push `b` into `adj_list[a]` and `a` into `adj_list[b]`.
Loop over nodes and print `i -> ` followed by all neighbours in `adj_list[i]`.
For a directed graph, delete the second `push_back`.
files.complexity: Time O(n + e) · Space O(n + e)
files.input_note: First line `n e`, then `e` lines `a b`.
files.output_note: Each line is one node and its neighbours in the order edges were read: `3 -> 1 2 4` means node 3 touches 1, 2 and 4.

check.q: Why does an adjacency list use less memory than a matrix for a sparse graph?
check.a: It stores only the edges that exist (about 2e entries) instead of all n² cells.

files.title: Edge list
files.what: Keeps every edge as a `pair<int,int>` inside one vector and prints them back.
steps: Create `vector<pair<int,int>> edge_list`.
Read each edge and `push_back({a, b})`.
Loop with `for (pair<int,int> p : edge_list)` (or `auto p`) and print `p.first` and `p.second`.
files.input_note: First line `n e`, then `e` lines `a b`.
files.output_note: One line per edge in input order. The arrow text `<-` is only decoration: `0 <- 1` is the edge (0, 1).
files.watch_out: The printed arrow points the wrong way for a directed edge `a → b`; it is just text, but keep it in mind so it does not confuse you.

check.q: Which later algorithm works directly on an edge list?
check.a: Bellman-Ford (and Kruskal's MST): they loop over all edges.

files.title: Extra practice: one graph, all three storages

problem.name: Module 1 extra practice - write all 3 representations of a 6-node graph

files.what: Reads the 6-node, 10-edge graph from the extra practice sheet once and stores it as an edge list, an adjacency matrix and an adjacency list at the same time, then prints all three.
steps: Nodes are numbered 1..6, so every array is made size `n + 1` and index 0 is simply not used.
The matrix `adj_mat` is cleared to 0 first, because a local array starts with garbage.
Each edge `a b` is read once and written three times: `edge_list.push_back({a, b})`, `adj_mat[a][b] = adj_mat[b][a] = 1`, and a `push_back` into both `adj_list[a]` and `adj_list[b]`.
The three storages are printed one after the other so you can compare their shapes.
files.complexity: Time O(n² + e) · Space O(n² + e)
files.input_note: The sheet's graph: `6 10`, then its 10 edges `a b`, nodes numbered from 1.
files.output_note: 10 edge lines, then a 6 x 6 symmetric matrix (row 2 `1 0 1 1 1 0`: node 2 touches 1, 3, 4, 5), then the list, where `4 -> 2 3 5 6` shows node 4 has degree 4. Count the 1s in the matrix: 20, which is 2e.
files.watch_out: With 1-based node numbers an array of size `n` is one too small: node 6 would write past the end. Size `n + 1` and loop `1..n`.

check.q: The matrix has 20 ones but the graph has 10 edges. Why?
check.a: The graph is undirected, so each edge sets two cells, `[a][b]` and `[b][a]`.

recap: Undirected edge = store it twice; directed edge = store it once.
Matrix: O(1) edge check, O(n²) memory.
List: O(n + e) memory, best for BFS/DFS.
Edge list: simplest, used by Bellman-Ford.
Number nodes from 0 so they can be array indexes.

check_yourself.q: A graph has 100000 nodes and 200000 edges. Matrix or list?
check_yourself.a: List. A matrix would need 10^10 cells.

check_yourself.q: In an adjacency list of an undirected graph, what is `adj[x].size()`?
check_yourself.a: The degree of `x`: how many edges touch it.

check_yourself.q: Draw any 4-node graph and write all three storages for it. How many entries does each have?
check_yourself.a: Matrix: 16 cells. List: 2e entries for undirected. Edge list: e pairs.

body: Put the word "graph" aside for a moment. Picture five towns, and the roads that join them. Town 0 has a road to town 1 and another to town 2. Town 1 and town 2 both have a road to town 3, and town 3 has a road out to town 4.
Drawn on paper it looks like this:

That picture is a graph. The towns are called **nodes** and the roads are called **edges**, and that is the whole vocabulary you need to start. The towns could just as easily be people and the edges "these two are friends", or web pages and links between them. Nothing changes.

You have already met a graph without being told. A binary tree is one: the nodes were tree nodes and the edges were the `left` and `right` links. A graph is the same idea with the rules taken away. **A tree could never come back to where it started; a graph can.** Look at the picture above: 0 to 1 to 3 to 2 and back to 0 is a loop. A node can also have any number of neighbours, not just two, and a graph can fall into separate pieces with no road between them. One more choice: if a road can be walked both ways the edge is **undirected**, and if it is a one-way street the edge is **directed** and only points one way.

Now the real question of this module. You can see the picture; the computer cannot. Before any program can answer "can I get from 0 to 4?" the graph has to sit in memory, and there are three ways to put it there. The plainest is to write the edges down exactly as they are read, as pairs. That is the **edge list**:

It is honest, and later algorithms that simply walk over every edge will want exactly this. But ask it the question a search actually asks, "who are the neighbours of 3?", and it has to read all `e` pairs to find out. With 200000 edges that is 200000 steps for one question.
The second way is a table with one row and one column per node. Put a 1 in row `a`, column `b` when there is an edge. This is the **adjacency matrix**:

Now "is there an edge from 1 to 3?" is one look, `mat[1][3]`, in O(1). The table is symmetric because each undirected edge was written twice, `mat[1][3]` and `mat[3][1]`; for a one-way edge you set only one of them and the symmetry breaks.

The price is the empty space. The table always has n² cells, even when almost all are 0: our five towns have 5 edges but 25 cells, and a graph with 100000 nodes would need 10^10 cells, which does not fit in memory at all.
So the third way keeps only what exists: for each node, a vector of its neighbours. This is the **adjacency list**, and it is the one every BFS and DFS in the next modules will use.

Three storages, one rule of thumb. Use the **matrix** when the graph is small or nearly full and you keep asking "is there an edge here?". Use the **edge list** when the algorithm only sweeps over all edges. Use the **adjacency list** the rest of the time: it costs O(n + e) memory instead of O(n²), and `adj_list[3]` hands you the neighbours of 3 straight away.

The four lesson programs below build these three storages from the same kind of input, `n e` followed by `e` lines `a b`, and print them back so you can see the shape of each one. The practice file at the end stores one graph in all three ways at once, so you can compare them side by side.
